# Assessment of owl limpet (*Lottia gigantea*) populations at sites within Crystal Cove State Marine Conservation Area

```{r load packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

```

## Project Summary:

This project serves to explore and analyze data on owl limpets collected from multiple sites throughout Crystal Cove State Park over the course of several years. Our aim is to conduct an initial exploration of the data to identify any interesting trends before engaging in full, in-depth analysis of multiple aspects of our data. The main research interests for this analysis will be evaluating the following: how limpet population density has varied both by site and by year across the region; how limpet shell length varies by site, depending on human disturbance, and by year; how the plot area of owl limpet territory varies in response to limpet body mass. Data visualization was done with ggplot2 from the tidyverse package, data set manipulation with dplyr from the tidyverse package, and statistical testing done via core R stats functionality.

You have been given data from several locations and survey years:

- 2022: Corona del Mar (CDM) - size data only, taken haphazardly

- 2023: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

- 2024: Heisler Park and Shaws Cove - size data in variable length transects, territories

- 2025: Treasure Cove (TC) - size data in 5-m transects, territories

```{r}
# Calling load() for limpet size data
load(file = "Data/SizeData_2022_2025.Rdata")

# Visual verification
SizeData_2022_2025

```

## Part 2: Population Density

For the population density analysis, we will analyze data from Shaws Cove, Heisler Park, and Treasure Cove. Create a data frame that excludes the Corona del Mar data, as that site did not have area measured.

```{r}
# Creating variable with Corona del Mar data removed by piping filter()
No_CDM_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site != "Corona del Mar")
```

#### 2.1. How many limpets did we measure at each site in each year for sizes?

Use nrow(), group_by() and count() to tally the limpet observations at each transect. We used the same transect numbers at Shaws and Heisler, so group_by() site as well.

```{r}
# How many did we measure total, across both sites?
nrow(No_CDM_Sizes)
# 1746 total

## How many did we measure at each site? 
No_CDM_Sizes |>
  count(site)
# 484 at Heisler, 793 at Shaws, and 469 at Treasure

# How many did we measure in each transect? 
No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(site) |>
  count(transect_num) |>
  knitr::kable()
# I'm not commenting this one out it's too long
```

#### 2.2 What was the limpet density (i.e., limpets per square meter) for each transect?

Make a new dataframe out of the `No_CDM_Sizes` that has a column called *density,* that calculates the limpets per square meter for each transect. Remember that the transect included 1 meter on either side of the tape (total of 2 meters wide). Make sure to maintain the separation in year for the two Treasure Cove surveys using the `group_by()` function.

```{r}
# Calculating limpets per square meter by mutating intermediate columns containing total limpet count per transect & transect area then mutating on a column divided by the results
Limpet_Density <- No_CDM_Sizes |> 
  group_by(year, site, transect_num) |>
  mutate(limpet_count = n()) |>
  mutate(transect_area = transect_length_m * 2) |>
  distinct(limpet_count, transect_area, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(limpet_density = limpet_count/transect_area) |>
  select(-shell_length_mm & -transect_length_m & -limpet_count & -transect_area)
# Converting resulting tibble with as.data.frame()
Limpet_Density = as.data.frame(Limpet_Density)

# Visual verification
Limpet_Density
```

Do you see any patterns just from examining this table of values?

Treasure Cove, broadly speaking, does seem to have generally lower limpet density per transect than either Shaws Cove or Heisler Park. All sites do have similar minimum densities but Treasure Cove's density doesn't reach as high on average.

#### 2.2. Calculating mean and standard error of population density

What was the mean limpets per square meter across all sites? And the standard deviation? And standard error?

```{r}
# Calculating summary statistics with summary()
Limpet_Density |> 
  summarize(
    mean_limpet_density = mean(limpet_density),
    sd_limpet_density = sd(limpet_density, na.rm = TRUE),
    sample_size = n(),
    se_limpet_density = sd_limpet_density/sqrt(sample_size)
  )

# mean = 3.338119, sd = 2.910088, se = 0.4544794
```

The mean limpets per square meter across all sites is 3.338119. The standard deviation for all sites is 2.910088, and the standard error is 0.4544794.

Now create a summary table in which you calculate separate mean and standard deviation for each site and year (Shaws vs. Heisler vs. Treasure Cove)? What was the standard error? Round the mean and standard error to one decimal place. (look up the `round()` function!)

```{r}
# use summarize() to calculate the mean and standard error (sd/sqrt(n)) for the two locations
LimpetPopSummary <- Limpet_Density |>
  group_by(site, year) |>
  summarize(
    mean_limpet_density = round(mean(limpet_density), 1),
    sd_limpet_density = round(sd(limpet_density), 1),
    sample_size = n(),
    se_limpet_density = round(sd_limpet_density/sqrt(sample_size), 1)
  )
 
# Display your summary nicely using kable(). 
knitr::kable(LimpetPopSummary)
```

Based on these plots, does your data meet assumptions for a t-test?

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)?

  Yes, all the data is continuous.

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population?

  The sample data has been randomly sampled from wild populations.

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)?

  All data except for the two Treasure Cove years vary similarly. The two Treasure Cove years do not vary similarly when compared to one another specifically, being roughly equivalent rather than having a similar degree of difference than either has from a non-self site.

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

#### 2.5 What is the sample size (of transects) for each site/year for our study of limpet population density?

Is it roughly the same so that we can compare? Is it enough to run a statistical test?

```{r}
# Measuring sample size with n() function called within summarize()
Limpet_Density |> 
  group_by(site, year) |>
  summarize(sample_size = n())
```

Sample size is roughly similar across all sites and years, having a range of 3 across minimum and maximum sizes.

#### 2.6. Does average number of owl limpets per square meter differ significantly between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove?

Filter the data to only include those sites before putting it into the `t.test()` function. These are a good comparison because they were measured in the same year with the same survey methods.

```{r t-test}
# run a t-test on your count data from each site (Limpet_Density)

# Creating variable for only Shaws Cove and Heisler Park data with filter()
ShawsHeislerDensity <- Limpet_Density |>
  filter(site == "Shaws Cove" | site == "Heisler Park")

# Running t.test() to conduct a Welch Two Sample t-test
t.test(limpet_density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerDensity)

```

Explain the results of this t-test. Are you surprised by this result, given the figure you made above? Why do you think the results are what they are?

Our t-test returns a p-value of 0.2629, meaning that there is not sufficient evidence to reject the idea that the true difference in mean density between Heisler Park and Shaws Cove is equal to zero. The two populations could only differ in our data by chance. This outcome was not too surprising – the column plot graphed above shows a large degree in overlap between the error bars for the two sites. If I had to guess, these results could be due to the two sites sharing the same environmental conditions. They could have similar levels of disturbance, similar distance from the highest point of the tide, or any number of factors placing their unique limpet populations under similar conditions.

#### 2.7 Did Treasure Cove population density differ between the two sample years? Do a t-test and make a graph to complement presenting the result.

```{r}
# Creating variable for Treasure Cove limpet density by filtering from Limpet_Density with filter()
TC_density <- Limpet_Density |>
  filter(site == "Treasure Cove")

# Running t.test to conduct a Welch Two Sample t-test
t.test(limpet_density ~ year, data = TC_density)

# Generating summary statistics for TC_density with summarize()
# Creating column plot using ggplot() + geom_col()
# Cleaning visuals with theme_bw(), theme() to remove gridlines and legend
# Adding error bar with geom_errorbar() using standard error from TC_Density
# p-value from t-test noted in subtitle
TC_density |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarize(
    mean_density = mean(limpet_density),
    sd_density = sd(limpet_density),
    n = n(),
    se_density = sd_density/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = year, y = mean_density) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean limpets per square meter",
    title = "Mean limpets per square meter at Treasure Cove each year",
    subtitle = "p = 0.4017"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = year), color = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
      ymin = mean_density - se_density,
      ymax = mean_density + se_density
    ),
    position = position_dodge(0.9),
    width = 0.2
  )

```

Since there was no difference in means, we'll ignore year at Treasure Cove from now on and just pool our data to make it easier for ourselves.

#### 2.8 EXTRA CREDIT: Do an ANOVA comparing Shaws, Heisler, and Treasure Cove 2025 density data (exclude 2023 so that the sample size is similar between all three). Use a Tukey post-hoc test. Explain the results.

```{r}
# Filtering out Corona del Mar data using filter()
ShawsHeislerTreasure_Density = Limpet_Density |>
  filter(year != "2023")

# Generating linear model between limpet density and site for Shaws Cove, Heisler Park, and Treasure Cove with lm()
model_SHT = lm(limpet_density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerTreasure_Density)

# Visualizing data to check for outliers and conduct a visual check for symmetry about median in each box
ggplot(ShawsHeislerTreasure_Density) +
  aes(x = site, y = limpet_density) +
  geom_boxplot()

# Checking QQ (which = 2 from plot() call) plot of residuals to check for normality
plot(model_SHT, which = 2)

# Shapiro-Wilk test on residuals (for fun, sample size is large) using shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(model_SHT$residuals)
# Likely to be a false positive

# Bartlett Test (bartlett.test) to confirm homogeneity of variance
bartlett.test(limpet_density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerTreasure_Density)

# Saving ANOVA table as variable using oneway.test to circumvent lack of homogeneity of variance
model_SHT_ANOVA = oneway.test(limpet_density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerTreasure_Density)

# Visual verification
model_SHT_ANOVA

# Doing post-hoc test (Tukey Test) via TukeyHSD
TukeyHSD(aov(limpet_density ~ site, data = ShawsHeislerTreasure_Density))
```

Our Tukey HSD results show a significant p-value for the Treasure Cove and Shaws Cove comparison only (p = 0.0065485), with the Shaws-Heisler and Treasure-Heisler comparisons both returning p-values over our threshold of 0.05 (p = 0.3478622 and p = 0.1763590, respectively). We can thus infer that Shaws Cove and Treasure Cove likely have differing mean limpets per square meter than one another, while the measured difference between the Heisler Park mean does not significantly differ from the mean densities at either Shaws or Treasure Cove.

## Part 3: Size

#### 3.1 Summary Statistics

##### 3.1.1 How variable were limpet shell lengths at each site and sample year? What is the sample size at each site?

```{r summary statistics }
# generate a nice table (like you did for counts, using kable() and round digits) with the mean shell length, standard deviation, and sample size of each site. Ignore transect. 

# Generating summary statistics per site and year by piping summarize() into group_by()
# Rounding calculations with round() call in summarize() arguments
shell_length_summary = SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  group_by(site, year) |>
  summarize(
    mean_shell_length = round(mean(shell_length_mm), 1),
    sd_shell_length = round(sd(shell_length_mm), 1),
    sample_size = n()
  )

# Using knitr to create a pretty table
knitr::kable(shell_length_summary)

```

##### 3.1.2 Graph the shell lengths at each site using a boxplot. What do you observe?

```{r}
# Creating box plot with ggplot() + geom_boxplot()
# Cleaning visuals with theme_bw() and theme() to remove gridlines
ggplot(SizeData_2022_2025) +
  aes(x = site, y = shell_length_mm) +
  labs(
    x = "Site name",
    y = "Shell length (in millimeters)",
    title = "Limpet shell length variance at each site"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  geom_boxplot()

```

#### 3.2. Is there a [statistically significant]{.underline} difference in [mean]{.underline} size between limpets measured at Treasure Cove (a relatively low-impact site) compared to CDM (a high impact site)?

We have a much larger sample size for shell lengths than we did for density, so we can apply our tests of assumptions more rigorously and demonstrate our various tests.

##### 3.2.1 [Determine whether a parametric or non-parametric test is appropriate.]{.underline}

T-Test assumptions (for a Student's T-test)

- Are the data continuous (i.e., not categorical/discrete)? **YES**

- Have the sample data been randomly sampled from a population? **(Yes)**

- Is there homogeneity of variance (i.e., the variability of the data in each group is similar)? **NO**

```{r}
## Test for Homogeneity of Variance with an F-Test

# create the appropriate filter to include only Treasure Cove and CDM data
CDM_TC_Sizes <- SizeData_2022_2025 |> 
  filter(site == "Treasure Cove" | site == "Corona del Mar")

# set the linear model for testing the assumptions
model <- lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, CDM_TC_Sizes)

# Examine plot of Residuals vs. Fitted values
plot(model, which = 1)

# F-test for homogeneity of variance - if p-value < 0.05 then variances are different. 
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)
# Fails :( p = 4.503e-09

# NOTE: if your sample fails this test, have no fear! Welch's t-test (the default that R uses) is okay to use with unequal variances. 

```

- Is the distribution of the model residuals approximately normal?

```{r}
## Test for normality

# examine a QQ-plot
plot(model, which = 2)

# conduct a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals
shapiro.test(model$residuals)

```

Why will we not pay attention to this Shapiro-Wilk test result? Because the sample size is very large and Shapiro-Wilk is overly sensitive (gives false positives) at large sample sizes.

##### 3.2.2 [Conduct the test]{.underline}

```{r t-test or Wilcox}
# calculate the t-test results
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = CDM_TC_Sizes)

```

#### [3.3 Graph your results using a column plot with error bars for standard error]{.underline}

For full credit, have well centered error bars and professionally labeled axes (they should not say "mean", they should say the variable name).

```{r}
# Generating summary statistics per site by piping summarize() into group_by()
# Creating column plot with ggplot() + geom_col()
# Cleaning visuals with theme_bw(), theme() to remove gridlines and legend
# Adding error bar with geom_errorbar() using standard error from CDM_TC_Sizes summary statistics
CDM_TC_Sizes |> 
  group_by(site) |>
  summarize(mean_shell_size = mean(shell_length_mm),
            sd_shell_size = sd(shell_length_mm),
            n = n(),
            se_shell_size = sd_shell_size/sqrt(n)
            ) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = site, y = mean_shell_size) +
  labs(
    x = "Site",
    y = "Mean shell size (mm)",
    title = "Mean limpet shell size at Corona del Mar and Treasure Cove",
    subtitle = "p < 2.2e-16"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = site), color = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
      ymin = mean_shell_size - se_shell_size,
      ymax = mean_shell_size + se_shell_size
    ),
    position = position_dodge(0.9),
    width = 0.2)

```

#### [3.4 - Interpret and explain the results of your test]{.underline}

Are we pretty confident that these samples were drawn from different populations? Why is the standard error so small?

We can be reasonably confident that these samples were drawn from different populations, as the p-value from our t-test is significant at p \< 2.2e-16. The small standard error observed in our data is likely the result of the data being closely clustered around the mean for the two respective sites. Assuming our high degree of significance correlates to a distinct difference between the two populations depending on site, it would make sense for the measured sizes to vary closely around the mean for their respective sites if they truly are so different from one another.

#### 3.5 - EXTRA CREDIT: repeat this analysis to see if the same result holds for the comparison at Heisler Park (high impact site) vs. Shaws Cove (low impact site).

If you would like to test whether size differs by predicted human impact, at CDM and TC "near" means high impact and "far" means low impact. Heisler was our high impact site and Shaws was our low impact site.

```{r}
# Filtering for Shaws Cove and Heisler Park data using filter()
ShawsHeisler_Sizes = SizeData_2022_2025 |>
  filter(site == "Shaws Cove" | site == "Heisler Park")

# Creating linear model for shell size as a function of site using lm()
modelSH = lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, ShawsHeisler_Sizes)

# Visualizing model residuals vs. fitted line
plot(modelSH, which = 1)

# Conducting F-test
var.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = ShawsHeisler_Sizes)
# Fails - variance is not homogenous

# Visualizing QQ plot
plot(modelSH, which = 2)

# Conducting Shapiro-Wilk test on residuals
shapiro.test(modelSH$residuals)
# Ignored lol (sample size is sufficiently large for this to be a false positive)

# Conducting t-test for ShawsHeisler_Sizes
t.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = ShawsHeisler_Sizes)
# p < 2.2e-16

# Generating summary statistics per site by piping summarize() into group_by()
# Creating column plot with ggplot() + geom_col()
# Cleaning visuals with theme_bw(), theme() to remove gridlines and legend
# Adding error bar with geom_errorbar() using standard error from ShawsHeisler_Sizes summary statistics
ShawsHeisler_Sizes |> 
  group_by(site) |>
  summarize(mean_shell_size = mean(shell_length_mm),
            sd_shell_size = sd(shell_length_mm),
            n = n(),
            se_shell_size = sd_shell_size/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = site, y = mean_shell_size) +
  labs(
    x = "Site",
    y = "Mean shell size (mm)",
    title = "Mean limpet shell length at Shaws Cove and Heisler Park",
    subtitle = "p < 2.2e-16"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = site), color = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
      ymin = mean_shell_size - se_shell_size,
      ymax = mean_shell_size + se_shell_size
    ),
    position = position_dodge(0.9),
    width = 0.2)

```

#### 3.6. MORE EXTRA CREDIT: conduct an ANOVA to test for differences in shell length between all four sites. Show your tests for all assumptions and make a graph.

```{r}
# Generating linear model between shell size and site for all our data with lm()
model_all = lm(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = SizeData_2022_2025)

# Visualizing data to check for outliers and conduct a visual check for symmetry about median in each box
ggplot(SizeData_2022_2025) +
  aes(x = site, y = shell_length_mm) +
  geom_boxplot()

# Checking QQ plot of residuals to check for normality
plot(model_all, which = 2)

# Shapiro-Wilk test on residuals (for fun, sample size is large)
shapiro.test(model_all$residuals)
# Likely to be a false positive

# Bartlett Test (bartlett.test) to confirm homogeneity of variance
bartlett.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = SizeData_2022_2025)

# Saving ANOVA table as variable using oneway.test to circumvent lack of homogeneity of variance
model_all_ANOVA = oneway.test(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = SizeData_2022_2025)

# Visual verification
model_all_ANOVA

# Doing post-hoc test (Tukey Test) via TukeyHSD
TukeyHSD(aov(shell_length_mm ~ site, data = SizeData_2022_2025))

# Generating summary statistics per site by piping summarize() into group_by()
# Creating column plot with ggplot() + geom_col()
# Cleaning visuals with theme_bw(), theme() to remove gridlines and legend
# Adding error bar with geom_errorbar() using standard error from SizeData_2022_2025 summary statistics
SizeData_2022_2025 |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarize(
    mean_length = mean(shell_length_mm),
    sd_length = sd(shell_length_mm),
    n = n(),
    se_length = sd_length/sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = site, y = mean_length) +
  labs(
    x = "Site",
    y = "Mean shell length (mm)",
    title = "Mean limpet shell length at each site",
    subtitle = "Results from ANOVA denoted on columns"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = site), color = "black", position = position_dodge()) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(
    ymin = mean_length - se_length,
    ymax = mean_length + se_length
  ),
  position = position_dodge(0.9),
  width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    label = c("A", "A", "B", "C"),
    vjust = -0.75,
    size = 3
  )

```


#### 4.3 Calculate meaningful variables from our measured values

Create new columns for:

- territory area in square millimeters from the "`numbsquares`" column

- Limpet body mass from shell length (equation below is from Fenberg et al. 2013).

```{r}
# Appending columns for territory area and body mass with mutate()
All_Territories_area_mass <- All_Territories |> 
  mutate(area_mm2 = numbsquares * (19 * 19)) |>
  # create a new column for territory area in mm^2 using the "numbsquares" column
         # mesh = 19 mm x 19 mm 
  mutate(mass_g = 0.00009*size_mm ^ 3.0471)
  # create a new column for limpet body mass
  # formula: mass_g = 0.00009*length ^ 3.0471

```

#### 4.6. What important assumptions of tests of linear regression do these scatter plots fail? How can you tell?

```{r}

## write a linear model for the relationship, then use the plot() function on the model object to show the residuals vs. fitted values and QQ plots to assess your regression. 

# Setting linear model for All_Territories_area_mass with lm()
```

One way to transform data that has this shape is to apply a log-transformation. Logarithmic relationships are common in biology for mass, volume, or other spatial relationships.

#### 4.7. Plot the relationship between log-transformed mass and log-transformed area. Does this relationship meet assumptions?


#### 4.8. What is the formula for the best fit line for the relationship between territory size and body mass in owl limpets?

```{r linear regression test summary}
# Saving data from log_model regression to variable
log_model_lm = summary(log_model)

# Visualizing results
log_model_lm

# The formula is y = 0.89031ln(x) + 8.2116
```

**The formula for the best fit line can be extracted from the model summary. The two values in the Estimate column are the coefficients - (Intercept) gives the y-intercept, and the variable gives the slope.**

**log(area) = 0.8903 \* log(mass) + 8.2116**

**or**

**Y = 0.8903 + 8.2116**

#### 4.9 Compare the relationship we found to the original study.

```{r}
FenbergTerr
```

Explain your findings!

Our All_Territories data does exhibit a positive linear relationship between its log-transformed limpet body mass and log-transformed plot area. This is consistent with observed trends in log-transformed plot area vs. log-transformed limpet body mass from the original Fenberg dataset. We can thus infer that there is at least some relationship between the body mass of limpets and their territory area that results in a corresponding increase to plot area in response to increased body mass. Interestingly, the R-squared value for the All_Territories data is only is 0.4496 compared to 0.7411 for FenbergTerr, meaning the model from this most recent data can only account for 44.96% of the variance in plot size. This could just be due to expected statistical variation since the p-value for both is less than 2.2e-16 but it is still worth noting.

#### 5.2 Explore some aspect of the data you find interesting and ask a unique question.

```{r}
### We didn't investigate much of how habitat could impact limpet density, if at all, so I'll do that briefly here. I'm curious if open vs. patch could be a predictor of how dense limpet populations are at that location.

## Starting by visualizing data with ggplot() + geom_boxplot() and removing NA values with filter()
Limpet_Density |> 
  filter(habitat != "NA") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = habitat, y = limpet_density) +
  labs(
    x = "Habitat",
    y = "Limpets per square meter",
    title = "Limpets per square meter by habitat"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  geom_boxplot()

### This honestly seems like a potential nothingburger based on initial visualization (boxes are almost identical for the two habitats) so I'm just gonna launch straight into statistical testing. This should be some variant of a t-test.

## Cleaning data

# Removing NA values with filter()
Limpet_Density_clean = Limpet_Density |>
  filter(habitat != "NA")

## Checking prerequisites for Welch's T-Test vs. Wilcox Test

# Setting linear model for clean data with lm()
habitat_density_model = lm(limpet_density ~ habitat, data = Limpet_Density_clean)

# Visualizing residuals vs. fitted with plot()
plot(habitat_density_model, which = 1)

# Running F-test with var.test() to check for homogeneity of variance
var.test(limpet_density ~ habitat, data = Limpet_Density_clean)
# IT PASSED (p = 0.7203)

# Visualizing QQ plot with plot()
plot(habitat_density_model, which = 2)

# Conducting Shapiro-Wilk test on model residuals with shapiro.test()
shapiro.test(habitat_density_model$residuals)

### Since our QQ plot seems to have a curve and the data set is small enough that there's reason to not disregard our Shapiro-Wilk test results, we'll assume non-normality and use a Wilcox test

# Conducting Wilcox test with wilcox.test
wilcox.test(limpet_density ~ habitat, data = Limpet_Density_clean)
# p = 0.3713

### Our p-value is much greater than 0.05 and we thus have no reason to reject the idea that the difference in mean limpet density between habitats is greater than zero. This strongly suggests that habitat may not play a major role in determining limpet density for a site. Unfortunately not a terribly surprising outcome given how similar the box plots were.

## Providing final visualization of results

# Generating summary statistics per site by piping summarize() into group_by()
# Creating column plot with ggplot() + geom_col()
# Cleaning visuals with theme_bw(), theme() to remove gridlines and legend

Limpet_Density_clean |> 
  group_by(habitat) |>
  summarize(mean_density = mean(limpet_density),
            sd_density = sd(limpet_density),
            n = n(),
            se_density = sd_density/sqrt(n)

  ),
```
